name: Plitvice Lakes National Park
blurb: Beech-fir forest and mossy tufa dams that hold back a chain of lakes.

tip.title: Remove the wolves
tip.text: Wolves and lynx both hunt roe deer. Set Grey wolf to -100% and watch roe deer, then the beech they browse and the ravens that feed on kills.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage: Plitvice Lakes National Park

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Light reaching the forest floor and the clear lake water drives growth of trees, mosses and algae.

nodes.name: Heavy rainfall
nodes.desc: The area gets about 1,500 mm of precipitation a year, which feeds the rivers that form the lakes.

nodes.name: Lime-rich karst water
nodes.desc: Water running through limestone and dolomite becomes loaded with calcium carbonate, the material of the tufa barriers.

nodes.name: Forest soil and nutrients
nodes.desc: Leaf litter and dead wood break down into the nutrients that feed the beech and fir forest.

nodes.name: Fungi and decomposers
nodes.desc: Fungi, bacteria and soil animals recycle fallen leaves, wood and carcasses back into the soil.

nodes.name: European beech
nodes.desc: Dominant tree of the park forests, which Wikipedia says cover about three quarters of the area. Its seeds feed dormice, squirrels, voles, deer and bears.

nodes.name: Silver fir
nodes.desc: Grows with beech in the old-growth stands of Corkova uvala, where some trees are about 700 years old. Its seeds are food for squirrels.

nodes.name: Mosses
nodes.desc: Mosses, with algae and bacteria, give tufa a surface to build on. They help trigger the limestone deposits that form the barriers.

nodes.name: Algae and cyanobacteria
nodes.desc: Films of algae coat stones and tufa in the lakes and streams and are grazed by insect larvae and small crustaceans.

nodes.name: European roe deer
nodes.desc: Browses beech, herbs and shrubs. It is the main prey of the lynx in Europe and a regular prey of wolves.

nodes.name: Edible dormouse
nodes.desc: A tree-dwelling rodent that eats beech seeds and fruit and hibernates in winter.

nodes.name: Bank vole
nodes.desc: A common small forest rodent of the park area that eats seeds, fruit and green plants and feeds many predators.

nodes.name: Eurasian red squirrel
nodes.desc: Feeds on tree seeds such as beech nuts and fir seeds.

nodes.name: Freshwater shrimps
nodes.desc: Small amphipod crustaceans that shred leaves and graze algae in streams and lake shallows. A favourite food of the dipper.

nodes.name: Caddisfly larvae
nodes.desc: Aquatic larvae that graze algae and plant matter on stones and are food for trout and dippers.

nodes.name: European badger
nodes.desc: An omnivore that eats earthworms, small mammals, amphibians and fruit. Recorded in the area.

nodes.name: Common raven
nodes.desc: A scavenger that feeds on carcasses of deer and other animals killed by predators or the winter.

nodes.name: Brown trout
nodes.desc: Wikipedia says two native brown trout forms live in the lakes. They feed on aquatic invertebrates.

nodes.name: White-throated dipper
nodes.desc: Walks into fast streams to feed on caddis larvae, shrimps and other invertebrates, and sometimes on small fish.

nodes.name: Eurasian otter
nodes.desc: Hunts fish, frogs and other water animals in rivers and lakes.

nodes.name: Grey wolf
nodes.desc: One of three large carnivores in the park. In Europe it hunts mainly roe deer, red deer and wild boar and also eats carrion.

nodes.name: Brown bear
nodes.desc: An omnivore that eats mostly plant food, including beech nuts, plus insects, small mammals and deer, and carrion in spring.

nodes.name: Eurasian lynx
nodes.desc: Hunts mainly roe deer in Europe and also hares. May be pushed to smaller prey where wolves are numerous.
